Musical parody can mean reworking an existing composition or imitating music for comic effect.
Modelling uses another work’s musical plan or pattern as a starting point for a new composition.
An homage is a piece written in honour of someone, sometimes borrowing their style or favourite forms.
A transcription adapts a piece for different instruments or voices.
Evidence status tells the reader whether a claim is documented, inferred or disputed.
A perfect cadence closes a phrase by moving from the dominant chord to the tonic.
A half cadence ends a phrase on the dominant chord.
A deceptive cadence moves from the dominant to a chord other than the tonic, usually the chord on the sixth degree, delaying the close.
A plagal cadence moves from the subdominant chord to the tonic, as in many settings of ‘Amen’.
Elision overlaps the end of one musical phrase or section with the beginning of the next.
A pivot chord belongs to both the old key and the new one, and the music modulates through it.
Common-tone modulation connects two keys through a note that belongs to both the old and the new harmony.
Direct modulation moves into a new key without a connecting passage or pivot chord.
Enharmonic reinterpretation gives a note or chord a new spelling and harmonic role while keeping its sounding pitch.
A chromatic slide moves a note or chord by a semitone into a new harmonic setting.
A sequence repeats a melodic or harmonic pattern at successively higher or lower pitches.
